title: Blockchain Projects: Build 5 Real-World Applications
tagline: A token system, certificate verification, a voting demonstration, NFT ticketing and a records registry, packaged as an honest portfolio
summary: A project-based course that builds five complete applications as learning projects on a test network: a token system with a funded vesting vault, privacy-respecting certificate verification, a transparent and a commit-and-reveal ballot, NFT event tickets with check-in, and a registrar-controlled records registry. Each project comes with compiled Solidity, tests to write, a threat model and honest claims, and the course ends with packaging your work as a portfolio. These are learning projects: none is audited or suitable for real value, real elections or legal records.

modules.title: Project craft: scope, build, present
modules.summary: How to choose a project that can be finished, structure the repository, document honestly and show your judgement.
modules.outcome: You can scope a project, set up a repository that others can run and write about it honestly.
modules.intro: A portfolio is not a collection of code; it is evidence of how you think. Reviewers look for finished work, clear scope, tests, honest limits and signs that you understand risk. This module sets the habits that make the five projects count.

topics.title: What reviewers look for
topics.html:
Signals that impress
SignalWhy it matters
The project works and a stranger can run itFinished beats ambitious
A short, clear READMEShows you can communicate
Tests, including the awkward casesShows you think about failure
Honest limits and a threat modelShows judgement and maturity
Small, focused scopeShows you can decide
A live demo on a test networkProof, not claims
Clean commits and structureShows professional habits
Signals that hurt
SignalWhy it hurts
Claims of 'secure' or 'production-ready' without proofOverclaiming destroys trust
A token launched to the public as an investmentIrresponsible and often unlawful
Copied code you do not understandInterviewers will ask
No testsSuggests you have not thought about failure
Secrets in the repositoryA basic security failure
Ten half-finished projectsBreadth without depth

Check what you just learned

1. Which impresses reviewers more?
  • A huge unfinished platform
  • A project with no README
  • A token with a big logo
  • A small project that works, is tested and states its limits (correct)

Finished and honest wins.

Check what you just learned

1. A threat model shows:
  • Judgement about risk (correct)
  • A logo
  • A token
  • Speed

You thought about what could go wrong.
keyPoints: Reviewers value finished, tested, honest and clearly explained work.
Overclaiming and unfinished sprawl hurt.

topics.title: Scoping and structure
topics.html:
A repository others can run
Folder or filePurpose
contracts/Solidity source
test/Automated tests
scripts/Deployment and helper scripts
web/ or app/The user interface
docs/Brief, threat model and decisions
README.mdWhat it is, what it is not, how to run it
.env.exampleNames of required variables, never real secrets
.gitignoreKeeps secrets and build output out of the repository

Scoping rules

  1. One clear user and one clear job.
  2. A written list of what the project will not do.
  3. A finish line you can describe in one sentence.
  4. Cut features, never tests.
  5. Prefer depth in one project to breadth across five.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with the user interface and discovering the contract does not fit.
  • Adding features because they are interesting rather than needed.
  • Skipping the README until the end, when you are tired.

Check what you just learned

1. What should be cut first when time runs short?
  • Tests
  • Nice-to-have features (correct)
  • The README
  • The threat model

Protect quality, cut scope.

Check what you just learned

1. .env.example contains:
  • Passwords
  • Private keys
  • Variable names without real secrets (correct)
  • Nothing

It documents configuration safely.
keyPoints: Scope small, write what you will not do, and keep a repository others can run.
Cut features, never tests.

topics.title: Writing it up honestly
topics.html:
What a good README answers
QuestionWhere
What is it?First paragraph
Why does it exist?The problem statement
What is it not?A clear limits section
How do I run it?Numbered steps
How does it work?A short architecture note
How secure is it?Threat model and known limits
What is next?Future work

Honesty about limits is a strength, not a weakness. A reviewer who sees 'not audited, test network only, key compromise is the main risk' knows you understand the field. A reviewer who sees 'unhackable' knows you do not.

Check what you just learned

1. Why state what a project is not?
  • To reduce marketing
  • It makes the README longer
  • It is required by Git
  • It shows honesty and prevents misuse (correct)

Limits build trust.

Check what you just learned

1. Claims such as 'unhackable' are:
  • Red flags (correct)
  • Impressive
  • Required
  • Expected

No honest builder says that.

Key terms: flip and sort

Scope
What a project will and will not do
Threat model
A structured list of what could go wrong
README
The project's front page
Repository
The folder of project files under version control
Test network
A public network without real value
Portfolio
A collection of evidence of your skills
keyPoints: A README says what it is, is not, how to run it and the known limits.
Honest limits earn trust.

modules.title: Project 1: a token system with distribution
modules.summary: A fixed-supply token and a vesting vault that releases tokens on schedules, with tests, risks and honest limits.
modules.outcome: You can build, test and explain a token with a funded vesting vault.
modules.intro: The first project is the classic: a token and the rules for handing it out. The twist is professionalism: a supply that cannot grow, promises that are always funded, schedules that people can verify and a clear statement that it is a learning project and not an investment.

topics.title: Design and contracts
topics.html:
Design decisions
DecisionReason
Supply minted once; no mint functionNobody can dilute holders
Burnable by holdersPeople may destroy their own tokens
Vault checks funding before each grantEvery promise is already backed by tokens in the vault
Per-person cliff and durationDifferent roles need different schedules
claim() pulls the vested amount minus claimedNo loops, no batches, no failure for others
Claimed is updated before the transferPrevents reentrancy
Custom errorsCheaper and clearer failures

Check what you just learned

1. Why must the vault be funded before creating a grant?
  • To save gas
  • A grant is a promise; an unfunded promise could never be kept (correct)
  • The compiler requires it
  • To hide balances

Promises must be backed.

Check what you just learned

1. A claim function that pulls its own vested amount avoids:
  • Events
  • All gas costs
  • Loops over many beneficiaries (correct)
  • Roles

Simple and safe.
keyPoints: Fixed supply and funded promises build trust.
Pull-based claims avoid loops and failures.

topics.title: Testing and risks
topics.html:
Tests for the vault

  1. A grant fails if the vault is not funded.
  2. Nothing can be claimed before the cliff.
  3. Exactly the right amount can be claimed halfway through.
  4. Everything can be claimed at the end, and not more.
  5. A second grant for the same address is refused.
  6. Only the admin can create grants.
  7. Claiming twice in a row pays nothing the second time.
  8. A fuzz test checks that claimed never exceeds total.
Risks and mitigations
RiskMitigation
Admin key stolen: attacker creates a grant to themselvesFund the vault only with what is planned; use a multi-signature admin; grants are limited by the funding
A beneficiary loses their keyDecide in advance whether a recovery policy exists; none is built here, and that is stated
Rounding in the vesting formulaRound down in favour of the vault; test the edge cases
Strange tokens (fees, callbacks)Use SafeERC20 and test with the real token only
Misleading marketingState plainly that this is a learning project, not an investment

Vesting calculator

Change the grant, cliff and elapsed months to see what is claimable. A teaching tool.

Adjust Grant (tokens), Cliff (months), Duration (months), Months elapsed and see Vested tokens (ignoring the cliff rule), Monthly release change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test that claimed never exceeds total?
  • It is easy
  • Fees depend on it
  • Tests must be long
  • A bug there would pay out more than was promised (correct)

An invariant protects the funds.

Check what you just learned

1. Tokens that nobody should be able to create more of need:
  • No mint function (correct)
  • A faster chain
  • More roles
  • Bigger fees

Fixed supply.
keyPoints: Test cliffs, edges, repeated claims and permissions.
State recovery and key risks honestly.

topics.title: Distribution and presentation
topics.html:
Ways to hand out tokens in a learning project
MethodUseCare
Vesting vaultTeam and adviser grantsFunded, scheduled, transparent
Merkle claimA community airdrop to a known listEligibility rules and deadlines
Direct transfers from the treasuryA few recipientsGas and record keeping
Faucet on a test networkLetting visitors try the tokenRate limits

What to show in the portfolio

  • A diagram of token flows from treasury to holders.
  • A table of allocations and schedules.
  • The tests and what they cover.
  • A statement that the token has no value and is not an investment.
  • A short video or live link on a test network.
  • The risks you considered.
Watch out

Do not launch a token to the public as part of a portfolio project. Treat it as a learning exercise on a test network.

Check what you just learned

1. Where should a portfolio token live?
  • On the main network with a marketing campaign
  • On a test network with a clear statement that it has no value (correct)
  • In a bank
  • Nowhere

Responsible practice.

Check what you just learned

1. A faucet is useful on:
  • A phone
  • A bank
  • A test network (correct)
  • The main network

Free test tokens.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fixed supply
A total that can never grow
Vesting vault
A contract that releases tokens over time
Funded
Backed by tokens already held
Invariant
A property that must always hold
Faucet
A service giving free test tokens
Allocation
How tokens are divided
keyPoints: Show allocations, schedules, tests and honest statements.
Keep portfolio tokens on test networks.

modules.title: Project 2: on-chain certificate verification
modules.summary: A registry that stores only fingerprints, roles for issuers, revocation and a verification page that never uploads the document.
modules.outcome: You can build and explain a privacy-respecting certificate verification system.
modules.intro: Certificates are the most honest use of a blockchain: public verification of a fact issued by a known authority. The craft is in what you leave out: no personal data, no pretence of replacing the law, and clear handling of mistakes.

topics.title: The registry contract
topics.html:
Design decisions
DecisionReason
Store a hash, never the documentThe chain is public and permanent; fingerprints reveal nothing
ISSUER_ROLE for issue and revokeOnly authorised staff can create or cancel records
Admin role separate from issuersA multi-signature wallet manages staff
certId duplicates revertA record cannot be overwritten
Revoke is a flag, not a deleteHistory stays visible and verifiers see the revocation
verify is a free view callAnyone can check at no cost
Events for issue and revokeDashboards and monitoring

Check what you just learned

1. Why mark a certificate revoked instead of deleting it?
  • Deleting is impossible
  • It hides the issuer
  • It saves gas
  • The history stays visible and verifiers can see it was revoked (correct)

Transparency about corrections.

Check what you just learned

1. A fingerprint reveals:
  • Nothing about the document's content (correct)
  • The full document
  • The student's marks
  • The address

A hash is one-way.
keyPoints: Store fingerprints, not documents or personal data.
Revocation is a visible flag.

topics.title: The verification page
topics.html:
Why it is built this way
ChoiceReason
Hash in the browserThe document never leaves the visitor's device
Read-only providerThe page needs no wallet and no gas
Clear statuses: valid, revoked, not found or changedPeople know what to do next
Certificate number hashed with keccak256Fits the bytes32 key in the contract

Check what you just learned

1. Why compute the hash in the browser?
  • It is faster
  • The document stays private on the visitor's device (correct)
  • It is required by the chain
  • To save gas

Privacy by design.

Check what you just learned

1. A changed document produces:
  • No fingerprint
  • The same fingerprint
  • A different fingerprint (correct)
  • A token

Any change alters the hash.
keyPoints: Hash locally, query read-only and show clear statuses.
No wallet or gas is needed to verify.

topics.title: Threats, privacy and honest claims
topics.html:
Threat model
ThreatMitigationRemaining risk
Forged PDFFingerprint will not match the recordNone for this check
Fake issuer keyRole control; multi-signature admin; monitoring Issued eventsA stolen issuer key can issue fakes until removed
Wrong certificate number typedPage says not foundUsers may be confused; improve messages
Fake verification sitePublish one official address; sign the pagePhishing remains possible
Privacy of the holderNo personal data on-chainCertificate numbers could be linked to identities elsewhere
Issuing to the wrong person by mistakeRevocationA window of misuse before revocation

Honest claims for the README

  • Proves that the college issued a document with this exact fingerprint.
  • Does not prove the education was good or that the holder earned it fairly.
  • Does not replace the college's legal records.
  • Depends on the security of the issuer's keys.
  • Records on a public chain cannot be erased.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the system actually prove?
  • The graduate is clever
  • Nothing
  • The college is accredited
  • This exact document was recorded by an authorised issuer and not revoked (correct)

A narrow, honest claim.

Check what you just learned

1. A stolen issuer key could:
  • Issue fake certificates until removed (correct)
  • Delete the chain
  • Change old records silently
  • Mint tokens

A real, stated limit.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fingerprint
A hash that identifies exact content
Registry
A contract that records entries
Issuer
An authorised creator of records
Revocation
Marking a record as no longer valid
SHA-256
A common hash function
Verification
Checking a claim against the record
keyPoints: A threat model lists each risk, mitigation and what remains.
Claim only what the system proves.

practical.title: Practical: issue and verify
steps: Deploy the registry and grant the issuer role.
Issue a certificate for a sample PDF.
Verify the same file and then a modified copy.
Revoke it and verify again.

questions.explanation: Personal data stays off the chain.

modules.title: Project 3: a decentralised voting demonstration
modules.summary: A simple ballot, a commit-and-reveal variant and an honest account of what blockchain voting can and cannot do.
modules.outcome: You can build a teaching ballot, explain commit-and-reveal and say clearly why this is not a secure election system.
modules.intro: Voting is where enthusiasm for blockchains meets the hardest requirements: secrecy, coercion resistance and trust in identity. This project builds a transparent ballot for low-stakes decisions and teaches you to explain precisely where it falls short of a real election.

topics.title: A simple transparent ballot
topics.html:
What the contract guarantees
PropertyHow
Only registered voters voteeligible mapping, set by the chair
One vote per addresshasVoted flag
A deadlineCompared with the block time
Public, auditable countstally mapping and Voted events
Valid options onlyBadOption check
What it does not guarantee
Missing propertyWhy
SecrecyEvery vote and address is public
Resistance to vote-selling and coercionA voter can prove how they voted
One person, one voteThe chair decides who is registered; identity is not solved
Protection from the chairThe chair registers voters and could add fake ones
Fairness of timingRunning totals are visible while voting is open

Check what you just learned

1. Why is this ballot unsuitable for a real election?
  • It uses Solidity
  • Votes are public, identities are not verified and the chair is trusted (correct)
  • It is too fast
  • It has events

Missing secrecy and identity.

Check what you just learned

1. hasVoted prevents:
  • Secrecy loss
  • Fake addresses
  • The same address voting twice (correct)
  • Vote buying

Not different addresses of the same person.
keyPoints: A transparent ballot enforces eligibility, one vote and a deadline.
It cannot give secrecy, coercion resistance or identity.

topics.title: Commit-and-reveal
topics.html:
What commit-and-reveal improves, and what it does not
ImprovesDoes not fix
Early results cannot influence later votersChoices become public after the reveal
Voters cannot change their mind after seeing othersVoters can still prove their choice to a buyer by sharing the salt
The tally is verifiableVoters who forget to reveal lose their vote
Identity of voters is still unsolved

Turnout and result

Change the registered voters and votes to see turnout and whether the result is valid under the rule: at least 50% turnout and a majority of votes cast. A teaching model.

Adjust Registered voters, Votes for A, Votes for B, Votes for C and see Turnout (%), Leader's share of votes cast (%) change.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the salt do in a commitment?
  • Makes the vote cheaper
  • Identifies the voter
  • Encrypts the chain
  • Stops others guessing the option by hashing each possibility (correct)

Without it the options are easy to try.

Check what you just learned

1. A voter who never reveals:
  • Is not counted (correct)
  • Is counted twice
  • Wins
  • Is fined

A drawback of the scheme.
keyPoints: Commit-and-reveal hides choices until voting closes.
It does not make the ballot secret or coercion-proof.

topics.title: Responsible framing
topics.html:
When it is reasonable to use such a ballot
SuitableUnsuitable
A student society choosing a nameA national or local election
A hobby group deciding a meeting dateVotes with legal consequences
A demonstration for a classDecisions where coercion or secrecy matter

What the README must say

  1. It is a teaching demonstration for low-stakes decisions.
  2. Votes and voter addresses are public.
  3. The chair controls eligibility and must be trusted.
  4. Real elections need legal frameworks, verified identity, secrecy and independent audit.
  5. Computer scientists broadly consider internet and blockchain voting for public elections unsolved and risky.

Saying clearly what your project is not will make it more credible. Interviewers will test whether you understand the gap between a smart-contract ballot and a trustworthy election.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is it a strength to document the limits of your voting project?
  • It makes the project longer
  • It shows you understand real election requirements (correct)
  • It hides bugs
  • It is required by law

It shows maturity and real understanding.

Watch out

Never present a blockchain voting demo as suitable for real elections.

Check what you just learned

1. Real elections need:
  • Only a smart contract
  • Only speed
  • Secrecy, verified identity and audit (correct)
  • Only a website

Far beyond a contract.

Key terms: flip and sort

Ballot
A collection of votes on options
Eligibility
Who is allowed to vote
Commit-and-reveal
Hide a choice first and show it later
Salt
Random data mixed into a hash
Quorum
The minimum participation for validity
Coercion
Forcing or paying someone to vote a certain way
keyPoints: Use such ballots only for low-stakes decisions.
State the missing properties plainly.

steps: Deploy Ballot with three options.
Register five voters and vote from each.
Try voting twice and as a stranger.

modules.title: Project 4: an NFT ticketing application
modules.summary: Tickets as NFTs with check-in, frozen used tickets, resale royalties and a realistic look at fraud and support.
modules.outcome: You can build a ticket contract with gate staff, explain its rules and budget the income.
modules.intro: Tickets are an honest use for NFTs: each is unique, ownership matters and verification at the door is a real problem. This project builds a ticket contract with a check-in role, freezes used tickets and looks at the practical issues that decide whether it would work.

topics.title: The ticket contract
topics.html:
Rules and why
RuleReason
Exact price and a supply capNo overselling and no accidental overpayment
GATE_ROLE can check tickets inOnly staff can mark tickets used
Used tickets are frozen in _updateA scanned ticket cannot be resold or reused
Unused tickets can be transferredFriends can share tickets before the event
Admin-only withdrawalOnly the organiser takes the proceeds
supportsInterface overrideBoth ERC-721 and AccessControl interfaces are visible

Check what you just learned

1. Why freeze a ticket after check-in?
  • To save gas
  • It is required by ERC-721
  • To hide the holder
  • A used ticket must not be sold or reused (correct)

Prevent resale of used tickets.

Check what you just learned

1. Only GATE_ROLE can:
  • Check tickets in (correct)
  • Buy tickets
  • View tickets
  • Burn tickets

Role-controlled.
keyPoints: Tickets are unique NFTs with a supply cap and exact price.
Used tickets are frozen so they cannot be resold.

topics.title: Practical problems of real ticketing
topics.html:
Problems and ideas
ProblemIdea
Gate staff need to verify ownership quicklyA signed, time-limited QR code made by the holder's wallet that the scanner checks against the chain
Screenshots and copiesRotating codes tied to a signature rather than a static image
Lost walletsDecide the policy before launch: no recovery, or a managed recovery with identity checks
Scalpers and botsPer-wallet limits, allowlists and price caps on resale
Refunds and cancelled eventsA refund function or a documented off-chain process
Non-technical buyersProvide wallet creation help and card payments through a provider if appropriate
Network feesChoose a low-cost network and show total costs honestly

These problems matter more than the Solidity. Many ticketing projects fail on the day because the entrance queue cannot verify tickets quickly or because buyers cannot get a wallet working. When you write about this project, spend time on the human flow.

Fraud thinking

  • What if two people show the same screenshot?
  • What if the scanner is offline?
  • What if a ticket is sold twice off-platform?
  • What if a gate staff account is compromised?
  • What if the event is cancelled?

Check what you just learned

1. Why does a rotating, signed code beat a screenshot?
  • It is prettier
  • A static image can be copied; a fresh signature proves control of the wallet right now (correct)
  • It uses less gas
  • It hides the ticket id

Prove control, not possession of a picture.

Check what you just learned

1. A cancelled event needs:
  • More gas
  • A new logo
  • A refund plan (correct)
  • A faster chain

Decide before launch.
keyPoints: Real ticketing fails on verification speed, wallets, fraud and support.
Use signed, rotating codes instead of static images.

topics.title: Economics and presentation
topics.html:
Ticket income

Change tickets, price, resale share and royalty to estimate income. A teaching model with made-up figures.

Adjust Tickets sold, Ticket price (rupees), Share resold (%), Average resale price (rupees), Royalty (%) and see Primary sales (rupees), Royalty income (rupees) change.

What to show in the portfolio

  • The flow from purchase to check-in as a diagram.
  • A short video of buying and scanning on a test network.
  • The tests, including double check-in and transfer after use.
  • A page that lists the problems above and your answers.
  • Honest limits: no real money, no audit, no legal advice.
Honest claims
You can sayYou should not say
Tickets are unique and verifiable on-chainFraud is impossible
Used tickets cannot be resold through the contractScreenshots can never be copied
Royalties are declared and can be enforced by the organiser's own marketplaceEvery marketplace will pay royalties

Check what you just learned

1. Which statement is honest?
  • Fraud is impossible with NFT tickets
  • Support is not needed
  • Nobody can copy a ticket
  • Tickets are verifiable on-chain, and fraud is reduced but not eliminated (correct)

Avoid absolutes.

Check what you just learned

1. Royalties are guaranteed when:
  • Sales happen on your own marketplace (correct)
  • Always everywhere
  • Never
  • On any chain

Otherwise they are optional.

Key terms: flip and sort

Check-in
Marking a ticket as used
Gate role
Permission for staff to check tickets in
Scalping
Buying tickets to resell at a high price
Royalty
A share of resale price paid to the organiser
Allowlist
A list of addresses allowed to buy
Frozen
Unable to move
keyPoints: Budget primary sales and royalties and show the human flow.
Claim only what the contract guarantees.

modules.title: Project 5: a records registry, and your portfolio
modules.summary: A registry with a trusted registrar, the line between technical and legal claims, and packaging all five projects.
modules.outcome: You can build a registrar-controlled registry, explain what it can and cannot claim and present five projects as a portfolio.
modules.intro: The final project is the one most tempting to oversell: records of ownership. A blockchain can keep a tamper-evident history, but ownership in the real world is decided by law and institutions. Building it honestly, and then packaging all five projects, is the last step of this course.

topics.title: A registry with a trusted registrar
topics.html:
Design decisions
DecisionReason
A REGISTRAR_ROLE approvesThe institution stays responsible; the chain records its decisions
Owner proposes, registrar approvesBoth the owner's intent and the registrar's checks are recorded
Details hash, not detailsPrivacy and permanence
Events for every stepA visible, tamper-evident history
No direct owner-to-owner transferReal-world rules must be satisfied first

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the registrar approve transfers?
  • To earn fees
  • Legal and paperwork checks happen off-chain and the institution stays accountable (correct)
  • The compiler requires it
  • To save gas

The chain records decisions; it does not replace them.

Check what you just learned

1. The registry's history comes from:
  • Fees
  • Colours
  • Events (correct)
  • Names

Public and permanent.
keyPoints: Owner proposes, registrar approves, events record the history.
Store fingerprints, not details.

topics.title: Technical claims and legal claims
topics.html:
What the code can and cannot say
StatementCan the contract support it?
This history of entries has not been secretly rewrittenYes: the chain is tamper-evident
Only the registrar approved this transferYes: role-based access control and events
This record matches the paper deedOnly as far as the registrar's check was honest
This person legally owns the landNo: law and the government register decide
The previous owner has lost all rightsNo: needs legal recognition

Many 'land on the blockchain' announcements promised more than they delivered because they skipped this table. A registry is valuable when it makes records transparent and harder to tamper with and when the surrounding institution and law recognise it. The code alone cannot create that recognition.

Questions to answer in your README

  1. Who is the registrar and why should anyone trust them?
  2. What happens if the registrar is dishonest or loses their key?
  3. Which law or rule makes the record meaningful?
  4. How are disputes and mistakes handled?
  5. What is stored publicly, and is that acceptable?

Check what you just learned

1. Can a smart contract make someone the legal owner of land?
  • Yes, always
  • Only on weekends
  • Yes if the fee is paid
  • No: law and institutions decide; the contract can only record decisions (correct)

Do not confuse records with rights.

Check what you just learned

1. A tamper-evident history means changes are:
  • Visible (correct)
  • Impossible to see
  • Free
  • Secret

Not necessarily impossible, but detectable.
keyPoints: Separate technical claims from legal claims.
Name the registrar, the governing law and the dispute process.

topics.title: Packaging the portfolio
topics.html:
For each of the five projects
ItemContent
One-line summaryWhat it does in plain words
Link to the code and a live test-network demoProof it runs
A diagramHow the parts connect
TestsWhat they cover and a coverage figure
Threat modelTop risks and mitigations
Honest limitsNot audited, test network only, what it cannot claim
What I learnedOne or two sentences of reflection

Presenting yourself

  • Lead with the project that best shows judgement, not the flashiest.
  • Keep every repository tidy, with no secrets.
  • Write short case studies for your best two.
  • Be ready to explain every line you wrote.
  • Say what you would do differently.
  • Link to the course badges and certificate if you have them.
Watch out

Never publish private keys, API keys or personal data in a portfolio. Check your repository history, not just the latest files.

Check what you just learned

1. Which should lead a portfolio?
  • The flashiest project
